message.content:
You are writing a concrete EXECUTION PLAN for a secondary-income business for Hooman (Adobe eng manager; $25-150K capital; ~10-20 hrs/wk alongside a day job; wants $5-30K/mo; already building CutLog).

IDEA: "License an engineered product design for royalties (inventRight model)"

The deep-research/validation stage produced these findings (JSON) — BUILD THE PLAN AROUND THE VALIDATED REALITY, not the original optimistic pitch:
{
  "idea": "License an engineered product design for royalties (the Stephen Key / inventRight model): invent simple high-volume consumer-product improvements, file cheap provisional patents, build sell sheets, cold-pitch manufacturers, collect ~5% royalties — as a low-cost, no-inventory, no-personal-guarantee secondary income stream.",
  "slug": "royalty_licensing",
  "assumptions_checked": [
    {
      "claim": "<$5K per idea to test (provisional patent + sell sheet + prototype), no inventory, no personal guarantee",
      "status": "VERIFIED",
      "evidence": "Stephen Key (the model's authority) puts it far lower: ~$100 provisional + ~$80 sell sheet = '$200 to see if your idea has legs.' Licensing means the OEM bears production/inventory/liability, so downside is capped at the per-idea spend. tim.blog/2007/11/27/how-to-rent-your-ideas-to-fortune-500-companies-part-ii/"
    },
    {
      "claim": "Monetizes an engineer's native output (product design)",
      "status": "PARTIALLY-TRUE",
      "evidence": "Design is an engineer's output, but the actual work is prior-art scanning, sell-sheet copy, cold-pitching '5 or 8 or 10+' companies per idea, and negotiation. Key steers inventors toward SIMPLE high-volume products, not deep-tech. The moat is persistence/volume of pitches — exactly the fragmented-buyer distribution weakness the Track-B report flags as Hooman's gap. Not his EE/AI strength."
    },
    {
      "claim": "Royalty ~5%, modest advances",
      "status": "VERIFIED",
      "evidence": "Key: 'a 5% royalty is most common for consumer goods. I usually ask for 7% and settle on 5%,' on WHOLESALE (~half of retail, so ~2.5% of retail). Corroborated: UpCounsel 3-6% of wholesale; MarketBlast 3-10% for consumer goods. tim.blog 2007."
    },
    {
      "claim": "$5-15K/mo across a portfolio after 18-36 months",
      "status": "FALSE",
      "evidence": "Survivorship-biased top-of-distribution outcome, not a base case. At 5% of wholesale, $10K/mo needs a product doing ~$4.8M/yr retail — a hit. Key's own cautionary example: a product that DID license earned only '~$6,000 annually.' His success anchors (Teddy Ruxpin $1M/mo) are lottery tops he cites to contrast. Getting to $5-15K/mo reliably needs a genuine hit; realistic ramp is 3-5 yrs or never."
    },
    {
      "claim": "Base rate of getting a product licensed via cold outreach is workable",
      "status": "UNVERIFIED",
      "evidence": "No clean public conversion rate; inventRight avoids stating one ('numbers game'). Nolo: 'Chance of licensing success is low... a struggle unless you have a connection.' Key's own protocol (pitch 5-10+ companies per idea, generate many ideas, expect most to die) is itself an admission the per-idea hit rate is low (<~10%); the model works by volume of shots, not hit rate."
    },
    {
      "claim": "inventRight itself: is it a coaching-upsell scheme?",
      "status": "PARTIALLY-TRUE",
      "evidence": "Not a classic invention-promotion scam (its free YouTube content is legitimately useful), but it IS a paid-coaching funnel: Coaching $3,495 / Gateway $6,999 / APEX $17,999 (inventright.com). Reviews 3.3/5 (~14 reviews); critics call it a 'money-grab,' cite $300/hr and pressure to buy more ('if I bought more books... they would help me'). The '<$5K/idea' pitch omits $3.5K-$18K tuition. You do NOT need to pay — the method is in Key's book."
    },
    {
      "claim": "Proof example: Lonnie Johnson / Super Soaker",
      "status": "PARTIALLY-TRUE",
      "evidence": "Real but a misleading outlier: NASA/JPL engineer, product hit $200M/yr and ~$1B cumulative, and he had to SUE Hasbro, winning ~$73M in 2013 arbitration for underpaid royalties. A billion-dollar megahit + litigation is the opposite of representative. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Johnson_(inventor)"
    },
    {
      "claim": "Proof example: Rotimatic",
      "status": "FALSE",
      "evidence": "Not a licensing story at all. Founders built Zimplistic (Singapore, 2008) and raised $16M-$42.5M of VC across ~5 rounds (Tracxn $16M; TheCompanyCheck $42.5M from Credence/EDBI/Openspace). It is the exact VC-funded hardware path the royalty model is meant to AVOID. Citing it as proof is simply wrong."
    }
  ],
  "competitors": [
    "inventRight (Stephen Key & Andrew Krauss) — dominant coaching brand, 25+ yrs, 10M+ YouTube views, programs $3,495 / $6,999 / $17,999",
    "MarketBlast — inventor-to-manufacturer submission marketplace (~1,500+ companies looking for ideas)",
    "Edison Nation / Inventors Launchpad ecosystem — submission/aggregator platforms that gate access and take a cut",
    "OEM open-innovation portals (Spin Master, Hasbro, P&G Connect+Develop) — the actual buyers, inundated, default to 'no'; they own the channel",
    "Long tail of invention-promotion scam firms (USPTO-warned) — charge thousands to 'evaluate' and deliver nothing; poison trust for cold outreach"
  ],
  "economics_verified": "Cost per idea: $200-$1,000 out of pocket (cheaper than the '<$5K' pitch), BUT add $0 (DIY) to $3.5K-$18K if you buy inventRight coaching. Royalty: 5% of wholesale ≈ 2.5% of retail (verified, on the smaller base). Per-idea odds of licensing: <~10%, a volume game (dozens of ideas to land a few deals). Typical licensed-product income: $0-$6K/YR each (Key's own drum-key example), not $5-15K/mo. To net $10K/mo needs one product doing ~$4.8M/yr retail — a hit. Downside: genuinely low, capped at a few $K + time (VERIFIED). BIGGEST CHANGE vs pitch: the '$5-15K/mo after 18-36mo' income claim — reframed as a near-free lottery ticket that MIGHT compound over 3-5+ yrs, not a reliable income engine. Also both cited proofs collapse (Rotimatic is VC-funded, Johnson is an outlier who had to sue for $73M).",
  "verdict": "PASS",
  "confidence": "HIGH",
  "kill_risks": [
    "Survivorship-biased income: base case is $0-low-thousands/yr per idea; $5-15K/mo requires a genuine hit most inventors never get",
    "It's a sales/persistence game, not an engineering game — hits Hooman's documented weakness (cold outreach to fragmented buyers) and does NOT leverage his EE/AI strength",
    "Time competes directly with CutLog for the same scarce evening hours — unlike a buy-and-operate asset that consumes capital + delegation",
    "Royalty enforcement risk: even megahits get shorted (Lonnie Johnson sued Hasbro for $73M); auditing/collecting from OEMs is ongoing adversarial work",
    "Coaching-upsell temptation: easy to sink $3.5K-$18K into inventRight chasing the dream; paid-tier ROI unproven (3.3/5, 'money-grab' complaints)",
    "Aggregators/OEMs own the deal-flow channel — you're one of thousands in the submission pile, no moat",
    "Both cited proofs are broken (Rotimatic is VC-funded not licensed; Johnson is an outlier + lawsuit) — a red flag about the underlying thesis"
  ],
  "best_niche_or_target": "Simple, high-unit-volume consumer-product IMPROVEMENTS (not deep-tech, not from-scratch inventions) in an un-sexy, fragmented category with many mid-size OEMs running open-submission programs — e.g. workshop/tools, EDC, pet, kitchen gadgets, or home-organization. Pitch via a one-page sell sheet + provisional patent to 8-15 manufacturers through MarketBlast plus direct OEM open-submission portals. Avoid toys (Spin Master/Hasbro gatekeeping + trend risk) and anything needing regulatory approval or custom manufacturing. Run it DIY from Key's book (skip paid coaching), as a near-zero-cost background bet with zero income expectation — never stealing hours from CutLog.",
  "_idea": {
    "slug": "royalty_licensing",
    "name": "License an engineered product design for royalties (inventRight model)",
    "claims": "<$5K/idea, no inventory, no personal guarantee; $5-15K/mo across a portfolio after 18-36mo; monetizes an engineer native output. Proof cited: Lonnie Johnson (Super Soaker), Rotimatic. Key open questions: what is the REAL base-rate of getting a product licensed via cold outreach? is inventRight itself a coaching-upsell scheme? typical royalty rates + advance? how many submissions to land one deal?"
  }
}

Also read your own research doc at /home/colligo/hs_scripts/claude/auto_research/runs/trackB/deep/royalty_licensing/01_research_validation.md for detail.

Write a concrete, realistic execution plan:
  - The specific target (exact niche/exam/tool/vertical/acquisition profile chosen in research).
  - First 90 days: week-by-week concrete actions, who does what, what gets validated when.
  - Months 4-12: path to the revenue target, hiring/delegation plan (this MUST stay part-time for Hooman).
  - Itemized budget within $25-150K; monthly burn; break-even point.
  - Revenue model + realistic ramp curve (subscribers/clients/deals over time).
  - Concrete go/no-go decision gates and the cheapest possible validation BEFORE committing real money.
  - How it coexists with CutLog for Hooman's limited hours (capital+delegation vs focus).

WRITE the plan to /home/colligo/hs_scripts/claude/auto_research/runs/trackB/deep/royalty_licensing/02_execution_plan.md (use Write). Return a ~200-word summary of the plan as your final text.

1	# Deep Research & Assumption Validation — "License an Engineered Product for Royalties (inventRight model)"
2	
3	**Date**: 2026-07-01. **Analyst**: Claude (Opus 4.8), skeptic mode.
4	**Idea (Track-B #4/#5, score 8.15)**: monetize an engineer's native output (product design) by
5	inventing consumer-product improvements, filing cheap provisional patents, building sell sheets,
6	cold-pitching manufacturers, and collecting royalties — the model taught by Stephen Key /
7	inventRight. Pitch claims: <$5K/idea, no inventory, no personal guarantee; $5–15K/mo across a
8	portfolio after 18–36mo. Proof cited: Lonnie Johnson (Super Soaker), Rotimatic.
9	
10	**Bottom line up front**: The *mechanics* of the pitch are largely TRUE (it really is cheap per
11	idea, no inventory, no PG, and the royalty rates/costs check out against the primary source —
12	Stephen Key himself). But the *income promise is survivorship-biased and the two "proofs" are both
13	misleading*: Lonnie Johnson is a billion-dollar outlier who had to sue for $73M, and **Rotimatic is
14	not a licensing story at all — it's a VC-funded hardware company that raised $16–42.5M**. The
15	realistic base rate is a low-single-digit hit rate per idea, most licensed products earn trivial
16	royalties (Key's own example: one product netted ~$6K/yr), and inventRight is a coaching business
17	selling $3,495–$17,999 programs. Verdict: **PASS as a standalone secondary income stream;
18	CONDITIONAL only as a near-zero-cost background hobby-bet** — which is exactly how the Track-B
19	report already framed it (#5, "compounding background bet," not a primary engine).
20	
21	---
22	
23	## 1. Claim-by-claim validation
24	
25	### Claim A: "<$5K per idea to test" — **VERIFIED (actually cheaper)**
26	Stephen Key's own numbers (the authority the whole model rests on):
27	> "$100 for a provisional patent application… $80 or less for a sell sheet created by a graphic
28	> design student… for many simple products your total costs are $200 to see if your idea has legs."
29	Source: Tim Ferriss / Stephen Key, tim.blog/2007/11/27/how-to-rent-your-ideas-to-fortune-500-companies-part-ii/
30	
31	So per-idea *out-of-pocket* cost is ~$200–$1,000 (add a cheap 3D-printed prototype). The <$5K claim
32	is comfortably true — **but only if you skip inventRight's paid coaching** (see Claim F). The real
33	"cost" is time, not money.
34	
35	### Claim B: "No inventory, no personal guarantee" — **VERIFIED**
36	Licensing = the manufacturer bears all production, inventory, distribution, and liability. The
37	inventor's downside is capped at the per-idea spend. This is genuinely the lowest-downside, most
38	capital-safe shape in the entire Track-B study, as the report states. No source dispute.
39	
40	### Claim C: "Monetizes an engineer's native output" — **PARTIALLY-TRUE**
41	Directionally true — product *design* is an engineer's output. BUT the licensing game is far more
42	sales/marketing/persistence than engineering: the work is prior-art scanning, sell-sheet copy,
43	cold-calling "5 or 8 or maybe even 10 or more companies" per idea (Key, same source), and
44	negotiation. The winning products are often *simple* consumer improvements, not deep-tech — Key
45	explicitly steers inventors away from novelty toward "high-unit-volume products." Hooman's EE/AI
46	depth is not the moat here; **persistence and volume of pitches is**. This is the same
47	"distribution to fragmented buyers" weakness the whole Track-B report flags as his one real gap.
48	
49	### Claim D: "Royalty ~5%, cheap advances" — **VERIFIED**
50	> "Royalty rates can range from .0001% to 25%… In my experience a 5% royalty is most common for
51	> consumer goods. I usually ask for 7% and settle on 5%." — Stephen Key (tim.blog, 2007)
52	Corroborated: UpCounsel "3 to 6 percent of the product's wholesale price"; MarketBlast "3% to 10%
53	of Net Sales for consumer goods." Royalty is on **wholesale** (~half of retail), so effective take
54	on retail is ~2.5%. Advances/minimum guarantees exist but are typically modest for unproven
55	consumer goods (often low-four-figures to low-five-figures; frequently just an advance against
56	future royalties, not free money).
57	
58	### Claim E: "$5–15K/mo across a portfolio after 18–36mo" — **FALSE / UNVERIFIED as a base case**
59	This is the load-bearing claim and it does not survive scrutiny. Do the math with Key's own numbers:
60	- A licensed product earning 5% of wholesale. To net **$10K/mo = $120K/yr in royalties**, the
61	  product must sell **~$2.4M/yr at wholesale (~$4.8M retail)**. That is a *hit* consumer product,
62	  not a typical one.
63	- Key's own cautionary example: a drum-key invention that *did* get licensed generated only
64	  **"approximately $6,000 annually"** — "insufficient return given the effort." (tim.blog, 2007)
65	- His success anchors are extreme outliers he names to *contrast*: Teddy Ruxpin "$1,000,000 in
66	  royalties a month." These are lottery tops, not the distribution.
67	So the realistic distribution is bimodal: **most licensed products earn $0–$10K/yr; a rare hit
68	earns six-plus figures.** Getting to $5–15K/mo reliably requires either one genuine hit or a
69	portfolio of ~5–15 modestly-selling licensed products — and *each* licensed product itself is a
70	low-probability outcome (Claim G). "18–36 months" to that number is optimistic; it assumes a
71	steady pipeline landing deals, which is not the observed base rate.
72	
73	### Claim F: Implicit "just follow the model" — inventRight is a COACHING-UPSELL BUSINESS — **VERIFIED (this is the real cost)**
74	inventRight's actual product ladder (from its own site, inventright.com):
75	- **Coaching Program**: $3,495 / 9 months
76	- **Gateway Program**: $6,999 (or 3× $2,450)
77	- **APEX Program**: $17,999 ("done-with-you")
78	Independent reviews (Trustpilot/smartcustomer, 3.3/5 across only ~14 reviews, 62% recommend) split
79	sharply: fans praise the free YouTube content ("HUNDREDS of hours of free videos… haven't paid a
80	single penny"); critics call it a "money-grab," cite **$300/hour** coaching, and report pressure to
81	buy more: *"they said if I bought more books or paid more money then they would help me."* Ripoff
82	Report entries allege fees of "$5,000–$20,000." Source: smartcustomer.com/reviews/inventright.com.
83	**Assessment**: it is NOT a classic invention-promotion scam (the USPTO-warned kind that charges to
84	"evaluate" and does nothing) — inventRight is *education*, and its free content is legitimately
85	useful. But it IS a paid-coaching funnel with real upsell pressure, and the pitch's "<$5K/idea"
86	conveniently omits $3.5K–$18K of tuition. **You do not need to pay them** — Key's method is fully
87	published in his book *One Simple Idea* and free articles. Treat the coaching as optional.
88	
89	### Claim G: "Base rate of getting licensed via cold outreach" (the key open question) — **UNVERIFIED but clearly LOW**
90	No one publishes a clean conversion rate, and inventRight avoids stating one ("licensing is a
91	numbers game"). Triangulated evidence that it's low:
92	- Nolo (legal encyclopedia): *"Chance of licensing success is low. Unfortunately, finding someone
93	  to license your invention can be a struggle, unless you have a connection to an entity willing to
94	  manufacture your product."* (nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/license-or-manufacture-invention-29775.html)
95	- Key's own protocol — pitch 5–10+ companies *per idea*, generate *many* ideas, expect most to die
96	  — is itself an admission the per-idea odds are low; the model works by *volume of shots*, not by
97	  hit rate. Practitioner rules of thumb in this community run around "1 in 10 to 1 in 20 ideas that
98	  you seriously pursue might license," and of those, most earn little (Claim E). Treat any single
99	  idea as <10% to license and a small fraction of *those* to be a meaningful earner. **Net: landing
100	  one economically-meaningful royalty stream can take dozens of ideas and 1–3 years.**
101	
102	### Claim H (proof #1): "Lonnie Johnson / Super Soaker" — **PARTIALLY-TRUE but a misleading outlier**
103	Real, but the opposite of representative:
104	- Johnson was a NASA/JPL aerospace engineer (1979–1991) who invented the Super Soaker
105	  (Wikipedia: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Johnson_(inventor)). He *did* license it (to Larami,
106	  later Hasbro).
107	- It generated **$200M in sales in 1991** and approached **$1B cumulative** — a category-defining
108	  megahit, not a typical improvement product.
109	- Crucially, he had to **sue Hasbro and won ~$73M in arbitration (2013)** for *underpaid royalties*
110	  — i.e., even a billion-dollar hit inventor got shorted and needed litigation to collect. This is
111	  a cautionary tale about royalty enforcement as much as a success story.
112	Using Johnson as "proof" is textbook survivorship bias.
113	
114	### Claim I (proof #2): "Rotimatic" — **FALSE (not a licensing story)**
115	Rotimatic (roti-making appliance) was **built and venture-funded**, not licensed for royalties.
116	Founders Pranoti Nagarkar & Rishi Israni founded Zimplistic (Singapore, 2008) and **raised
117	$16M–$42.5M across ~5 rounds** (Tracxn: $16M; TheCompanyCheck: $42.5M from Credence, EDBI,
118	Openspace Capital). It is the *exact* capital-intensive, VC-funded hardware path the licensing model
119	is supposed to *avoid*. **Citing it as proof of the royalty-licensing model is simply wrong** and
120	should be struck from the pitch.
121	
122	---
123	
124	## 2. Competitors / the "market" for this idea
125	
126	This isn't a market you enter so much as an activity, but the relevant players:
127	
128	- **Education/coaching incumbents** (who you'd compete with for attention *and* could pay):
129	  **inventRight** (Stephen Key & Andrew Krauss; 25+ yrs, 10M+ YouTube views, $3.5K–$18K programs) is
130	  the dominant brand. Others: **Rich Levandov / various "invention coaches,"** book authors, and a
131	  long tail of YouTube inventor-influencers.
132	- **Marketplaces / submission platforms**: **MarketBlast** (marketblast.com — connects inventors to
133	  ~"1,500+ companies looking for ideas," a figure inventRight also cites), **Edison Nation / Inventiv
134	  (now "Inventors Launchpad" ecosystem)**, and open-innovation portals run by big CPG/toy OEMs
135	  themselves (Spin Master, Hasbro, Procter & Gamble Connect+Develop). These aggregators own the
136	  best niche — the *deal flow to manufacturers* — and take a cut or gate access.
137	- **The buyers (OEMs)**: toy, houseware, tool, EDC, pet, and hardware manufacturers with
138	  "open submission" programs. They are inundated and default to "no." This is the "entrenched
139	  incumbent / aggregator owns the channel" pattern the Track-A research kept flagging.
140	- **Invention-promotion scams** (the anti-pattern the USPTO warns about): firms charging thousands
141	  to "evaluate/market" ideas and delivering nothing. inventRight is *not* this, but the space is
142	  full of them, which poisons trust and makes cold OEM outreach harder.
143	
144	There is no defensible niche to "own" here — the best sub-niches are just product categories where
145	you have taste (Key's advice: pick a category you know, e.g. workshop/tools/EDC/pet/home).
146	
147	---
148	
149	## 3. Best specific niche/target (from the data)
150	
151	The model works best on **simple, high-unit-volume consumer-product *improvements* in an
152	un-sexy, fragmented category with many mid-size manufacturers that run open-submission programs** —
153	NOT deep-tech. Concretely, the strongest fit given the founder + the data:
154	- **Category**: workshop/tools, EDC, pet products, kitchen gadgets, or home-organization — mature
155	  categories with hundreds of mid-size OEMs, low novelty risk, and high unit volume (Key: "that 5%
156	  on every unit can really add up").
157	- **Product type**: an incremental improvement to an existing high-volume product (not a
158	  from-scratch invention), sold via a one-page sell sheet + provisional patent, pitched to 8–15
159	  manufacturers via **MarketBlast + direct open-submission portals**.
160	- **Avoid**: toys (dominated by Spin Master/Hasbro gatekeeping + trend risk), anything needing
161	  regulatory approval, and anything requiring custom manufacturing you'd have to prove out.
162	- **His actual edge**: not EE depth, but (a) capital to file real provisionals/prototypes cheaply,
163	  (b) analytical filtering of which ideas have prior-art-clear, high-volume potential, and (c) the
164	  ability to run it as a true background portfolio bet without needing the income.
165	
166	---
167	
168	## 4. Re-derived realistic economics (what changed vs the pitch)
169	
170	| Metric | Pitch | Realistic (this research) |
171	|---|---|---|
172	| Cost per idea | <$5K | **$200–$1,000** out of pocket (Key). Cheaper than claimed. |
173	| Coaching cost | (omitted) | **$0 (DIY from his book) up to $3.5K–$18K** (inventRight). Optional; skip it. |
174	| Royalty rate | ~5% | **5% of *wholesale* ≈ 2.5% of retail** (verified, but on the smaller base). |
175	| Per-idea odds of licensing | (implied high) | **<~10%; volume game** — dozens of ideas to land a few deals. |
176	| Typical licensed-product income | $5–15K/mo portfolio | **Most: $0–$6K/*yr* each** (Key's drum-key example). A *hit* is rare. |
177	| Time to $5–15K/mo | 18–36 mo | **Highly uncertain; more likely 3–5 yrs, or never**, unless one product hits. Lumpy & back-loaded. |
178	| Downside | none meaningful | **VERIFIED low** — capped at a few $K + your time. |
179	| Time load | 5–15 hrs/wk | Plausible, but it's the *right* 5–15 hrs (sales/persistence), and it competes with CutLog for exactly the scarce focus the report warns about. |
180	
181	**The number that changed most**: the income claim. "$5–15K/mo after 18–36mo" is a
182	survivorship-biased top-of-distribution outcome, not a base case. The honest reframe (which the
183	Track-B report already made) is: **a near-free lottery ticket that *might* compound, not a reliable
184	$5–15K/mo income engine.**
185	
186	---
187	
188	## 5. Kill-risks
189	
190	1. **Survivorship-biased income** — the base case is $0–low-thousands/yr per idea; $5–15K/mo needs a
191	   genuine hit that most inventors never get. This is the killer for "secondary *income*."
192	2. **It's a sales/persistence game, not an engineering game** — hits Hooman's one documented
193	   weakness (cold outreach to fragmented buyers) and does NOT leverage his real strength.
194	3. **Time competes with CutLog** — the report's central finding is that time (not capital) is his
195	   constraint; this needs the *same* scarce evening hours CutLog needs, unlike a buy-and-operate
196	   asset that consumes capital + delegation.
197	4. **Royalty enforcement risk** — even megahits get shorted (Lonnie Johnson sued for $73M);
198	   auditing/collecting royalties from OEMs is real, ongoing, adversarial work.
199	5. **Coaching-upsell temptation** — easy to sink $3.5K–$18K into inventRight programs chasing the
200	   dream; the ROI on the paid tiers is unproven (3.3/5, "money-grab" complaints).
201	6. **Aggregators/OEMs own the channel** — you're one of thousands in the submission pile; no moat.
202	7. **Both cited proofs are broken** — Lonnie Johnson (outlier + lawsuit), Rotimatic (VC-funded, not
203	   licensing). A pitch resting on two bad proofs is a red flag about the whole thesis.
204	
205	---
206	
207	## 6. Verdict
208	
209	**PASS** as a standalone secondary-income stream (it will not reliably produce $5–15K/mo, and it
210	taxes his scarce focus while leaning on his weakness). **CONDITIONAL** only in the narrow framing
211	the Track-B report already gave it: a **near-zero-cost, ~a-few-hours background compounding bet**,
212	run DIY (skip paid coaching), on 1–2 simple high-volume product improvements in a category he
213	enjoys — with **zero expectation of it becoming income** and an absolute rule that it never steals
214	hours from CutLog. Under that framing it's a fine hobby-bet; as a "$5–15K/mo secondary income," it's
215	a survivorship-bias trap.
216	
217	**Confidence: HIGH** on the mechanics (costs, royalty rates, no-PG — all verified from the primary
218	source) and on the two proofs being misleading (Rotimatic disproven, Johnson clearly an outlier).
219	**MEDIUM** on the exact base-rate number (no clean public conversion rate exists; the "<10% per idea,
220	most earn little" conclusion is triangulated, not a single cited statistic).
221	
222	### Sources
223	- Stephen Key via Tim Ferriss — royalty rates, $200/idea cost, "5–10 companies," $6K/yr vs $1M/mo
224	  examples: https://tim.blog/2007/11/27/how-to-rent-your-ideas-to-fortune-500-companies-part-ii/
225	- inventRight program pricing ($3,495 / $6,999 / $17,999): https://inventright.com/
226	- inventRight reviews (3.3/5, ~14 reviews, "money-grab," $300/hr, upsell pressure):
227	  https://www.smartcustomer.com/reviews/inventright.com (Sitejabber mirror)
228	- Lonnie Johnson / Super Soaker ($200M/yr, ~$1B, $73M arbitration award):
229	  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Johnson_(inventor)
230	- Rotimatic funding ($16M–$42.5M, VC-funded — NOT licensing): Tracxn
231	  https://tracxn.com/d/companies/zimplistic/ ; TheCompanyCheck
232	  https://www.thecompanycheck.com/company/b/rotimatic/tjb1311jsny9byevo
233	- Nolo — "chance of licensing success is low":
234	  https://www.nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/license-or-manufacture-invention-29775.html
235	- Royalty-rate corroboration: UpCounsel (3–6% wholesale), MarketBlast (3–10% consumer goods)

# Execution Plan — Royalty Licensing (inventRight model)

**Date**: 2026-07-01. **Author**: Claude (Opus 4.8). **Owner**: Hooman Shariati.
**Status**: PASS as a *near-zero-cost background bet* — NOT as a reliable $5–30K/mo income engine.
**Companion doc**: `01_research_validation.md` (read it first; this plan is built on its verdict).

---

## 0. The honest framing (read this before anything else)

The validation research is unambiguous, and this plan does not fight it:

- **This will not reliably produce $5–30K/mo.** At 5% of *wholesale* (≈2.5% of retail), a single
  product must sell **~$4.8M/yr retail** to net $10K/mo. That is a *hit*. The base case for a
  licensed product is **$0–$6K/YEAR** (Stephen Key's own drum-key example). Per-idea odds of
  licensing at all are **<~10%**, and most of those earn trivial money.
- **Time is Hooman's binding constraint, not capital** — and this activity spends the *exact same*
  scarce evening hours as CutLog, while leaning on his one documented weakness (cold outreach to
  fragmented buyers) rather than his EE/AI strength.
- **Therefore this is run as a lottery ticket, not a business.** The correct posture: minimize
  cash AND time spent, cap total exposure hard, and treat any royalty as a windfall — never a plan.

**What this plan optimizes for:** the *cheapest, lowest-time-cost* way to buy a small number of
real lottery tickets (licensed-product shots) without (a) sinking money into inventRight coaching,
(b) stealing focus from CutLog, or (c) letting sunk-cost drag it past its kill-gates.

**If you want a $5–30K/mo secondary income, this is the wrong idea in the study** — a buy-and-operate
cash-flowing asset (capital + delegation) fits Hooman's profile far better than a persistence/sales
game. This plan exists only to run royalty licensing *correctly if run at all*: small, cheap, bounded.

---

## 1. The specific target (chosen niche)

From the research, the only defensible framing:

- **Category**: workshop/tools, EDC (everyday-carry), or pet products — mature, un-sexy,
  high-unit-volume, hundreds of mid-size OEMs running open-submission programs. **Pick ONE** category
  Hooman personally uses and has taste in (default recommendation: **workshop/tools** — he tinkers,
  understands the products, and can judge a good improvement).
- **Product type**: a *simple incremental improvement* to an existing high-volume product — NOT a
  from-scratch invention, NOT deep-tech, NOT anything needing regulatory approval or custom
  manufacturing to prove out.
- **Channel**: one-page **sell sheet** + **provisional patent** → pitched to **8–15 manufacturers**
  via **MarketBlast** (~1,500 companies seeking ideas) + direct OEM open-submission portals.
- **Explicitly avoid**: toys (Spin Master/Hasbro gatekeeping + trend risk), regulated products,
  anything requiring you to prove manufacturability, and **inventRight paid coaching** ($3.5K–$18K).
- **Hooman's real edge here** (small): capital to file real provisionals cheaply, analytical
  filtering of prior-art-clear high-volume ideas, and the ability to run it with zero income pressure.

**Concrete commitment for the pilot**: land **2–3 product improvements** through the full funnel
(idea → provisional → sell sheet → pitch to 10+ OEMs each) within **12 months**, spending
**≤$6K cash total** and **≤4 hrs/week**, using only free resources (Key's book *One Simple Idea* +
free YouTube). The pilot's job is to *test the funnel and Hooman's stomach for it* — not to hit income.

---

## 2. First 90 days — week-by-week

**Cadence rule: ≤3 hrs/week, and it goes to ZERO in any week CutLog needs the time.** This is the
backstop bet; CutLog is the priority.

**Weeks 1–2 — Learn the model for $0 (validation before any spend).**
- Hooman: read *One Simple Idea* (Stephen Key) + watch ~5–8 hrs of the free inventRight YouTube
  library. **Do not buy coaching.**
- Deliverable: a 1-page written summary of the process (idea → prior-art → provisional → sell sheet
  → pitch → negotiate) so the method is internalized, not re-learned later.
- **GATE 0 (stomach check)**: after this, honestly answer *"Am I willing to cold-pitch 30+ strangers
  over a year?"* If no → **STOP HERE, $0 spent.** This is the cheapest possible off-ramp.

**Weeks 3–4 — Pick the category + generate an idea list.**
- Choose ONE category (default: workshop/tools). Brainstorm 15–20 candidate improvements to
  existing high-volume products. Log them in a simple sheet (`ideas_log.md`/spreadsheet).
- Filter to the 5 most promising on: high unit volume, obvious pain, simple to describe on one page.

**Weeks 5–6 — Prior-art scan (the real kill filter, free).**
- For each of the top 5: free Google Patents + USPTO + Amazon/retail search. Kill anything already
  patented or already on shelves. Expect 3–4 of 5 to die here. **This is where cost is saved** —
  never file on an idea you didn't prior-art scan.
- Deliverable: 1–2 surviving ideas that look prior-art-clear.

**Weeks 7–8 — File first provisional(s) + first sell sheet.**
- File **1 provisional patent** (self-file via USPTO ~$65–130 micro-entity, or ~$300 with a light
  attorney review) on the single best idea. **Spend real money on ONE idea first, not all.**
- Commission a sell sheet from a design student / Fiverr (~$80–200). Optional: a cheap 3D-printed
  prototype photo (~$50–150).
- Running cash total to date: **~$300–650.**

**Weeks 9–10 — Build the pitch list + start outreach.**
- Set up a free MarketBlast account; submit the idea. Identify 10–15 direct OEM open-submission
  portals in the category.
- Begin cold outreach: submit/pitch to the first 5 targets. Track every touch in a CRM-lite sheet
  (company, contact, date, response).

**Weeks 11–12 — Finish first pitch wave + first review.**
- Complete pitches to 10+ manufacturers for idea #1. File provisional + sell sheet for idea #2 if
  time and budget allow (adds ~$300–650).
- **GATE 1 (90-day review)**: metrics = # ideas prior-art-cleared, # provisionals filed, # OEMs
  pitched, # of *any* reply (even "no"), and — honestly — hours actually spent + whether it hurt
  CutLog. Cash to date should be **≤$1.5K.**

---

## 3. Months 4–12 — the (deliberately modest) path forward

There is **no revenue-target ramp to promise** — the research forbids it. The month 4–12 goal is
purely to **complete the pilot** (2–3 ideas fully pitched) and reach a clean go/no-go, not to hit a
dollar number.

- **Months 4–6**: Keep idea #1 and #2 pitches alive (follow-ups, respond to any OEM interest). Add
  idea #3 through the full funnel. Provisional patents last 12 months — decide per idea whether to
  let it lapse (default) or convert to a non-provisional (~$1–3K, **only if a manufacturer is
  actually engaged** — never speculatively).
- **Months 7–12**: If any OEM shows real interest → negotiate (5% of wholesale ask 7%/settle 5%;
  insist on a minimum annual guarantee + an **audit clause**, given the documented royalty-shorting
  risk). If nothing lands → let provisionals lapse, harvest learnings, and stop generating new ideas.

**Hiring / delegation** (keeps it part-time — this is the ONE lever that makes it non-time-toxic):
- **Delegate the low-skill, time-heavy pieces with cash, not hours:** sell-sheet design (Fiverr,
  ~$100/ea), 3D-print prototype photos (~$100/ea), and — the big one — **prior-art search + outreach
  list building** to a **VA** (~$8–20/hr, ~$150–300 per idea batch).
- **Hooman keeps only**: idea selection, the go/no-go judgment, and the actual negotiation. That
  compresses his personal load to **~2 hrs/week**, which is the only way this coexists with CutLog.
- Do **not** hire anyone to *replace the cold-outreach persistence itself* early — a VA can build
  lists and send template submissions, but genuine OEM relationship follow-through needs the founder
  until a deal is warm.

---

## 4. Budget (itemized, hard-capped)

| Item | Low (DIY) | High (delegated) |
|---|---|---|
| inventRight coaching | **$0 (skip — use the book)** | $0 (still skip) |
| Book *One Simple Idea* | $15 | $15 |
| Provisional patents (2–3 ideas) | $200 (self-file, micro-entity) | $900 (light attorney review) |
| Sell sheets (2–3) | $200 | $600 |
| Prototype photos/3D prints (2–3) | $150 | $450 |
| MarketBlast / submission fees | $0–100 | $300 |
| VA (prior-art + outreach, 3 idea batches) | $0 (DIY) | $900 |
| Contingency (1 non-provisional IF a deal warms) | $0 | $3,000 |
| **TOTAL (12-month pilot)** | **~$600** | **~$6,200** |

- **Hard cap: $6K cash and 12 months.** This is *far* below the $25–150K study range — deliberately.
  The whole point is that the downside is capped at a few thousand dollars + time.
- **Monthly burn**: ~$100–500, lumpy (spikes at each provisional filing).
- **Break-even**: undefined/irrelevant by design. A *single* licensed product doing even ~$500K/yr
  retail (5% wholesale ≈ ~$6K/yr) repays the entire pilot; but base case is **$0 return**, and that
  outcome is acceptable and pre-accepted.

---

## 5. Revenue model + realistic ramp

- **Model**: 5% of *wholesale* (≈2.5% of retail) per licensed unit, ideally with a modest annual
  minimum guarantee + audit rights. Advances are typically small and against future royalties.
- **Realistic ramp (base case)**: Year 1 = **$0** (pilot; probably nothing licensed yet). Years 2–3 =
  **$0–low-thousands/yr** *if* one modest product licenses. A meaningful $5–15K/mo requires a genuine
  hit that **most inventors never get**, arriving lumpy and back-loaded on a **3–5 year (or never)**
  horizon.
- **Deals-over-time (honest)**: pitch ~30+ OEM touches across 2–3 ideas in year 1 → expect **0–1**
  license. Portfolio of ~10–15 lifetime ideas → maybe **1–2** ever license → maybe **0–1** earns
  more than pocket change. Plan around **zero**; treat anything else as a windfall.

---

## 6. Go/No-Go gates (cheapest validation first)

- **GATE 0 (Week 2, $0)** — *Stomach test.* After learning the model free: is Hooman willing to
  cold-pitch 30+ strangers/yr and accept mostly-"no"? **No → STOP, $0 spent.** (Cheapest possible
  validation, before any money.)
- **GATE 1 (Day 90, ≤$1.5K)** — *Funnel test.* Did idea #1 get prior-art-cleared, provisional'd,
  sell-sheeted, and pitched to 10+ OEMs? Did it stay ≤3 hrs/wk and NOT hurt CutLog? **Any "no" on the
  CutLog-impact question → STOP.**
- **GATE 2 (Month 6)** — *Signal test.* Across 2 ideas / 20+ pitches, has **any** OEM given a
  substantive reply (request for more info / sample / terms)? **Zero substantive interest → do NOT
  file more provisionals; finish existing pitches and wind down.**
- **GATE 3 (Month 12)** — *Continuation test.* Is any deal warm? **Yes → negotiate + optionally
  convert one provisional.** **No → let all provisionals lapse, close the pilot, write up learnings.**
  Total spend by here should be **≤$6K.**

**Absolute stop-loss**: if cash exceeds $6K OR Hooman's personal time exceeds ~3 hrs/wk for two
consecutive months OR CutLog momentum measurably slips → **halt immediately**, regardless of gate.

---

## 7. How it coexists with CutLog

The research is explicit: Hooman's constraint is **time/focus, not capital**, and this idea competes
for the *same* evening hours CutLog needs — its single biggest kill-risk. Rules:

1. **CutLog always wins the hour.** Royalty work is the *residual* — only the hours CutLog doesn't
   need that week. Some weeks that's zero, and that's fine.
2. **Buy down the time with money, not the reverse.** Every delegable task (design, prints,
   prior-art, list-building, template outreach) goes to Fiverr/VA. Hooman's personal footprint stays
   **≤2 hrs/wk** — idea selection, go/no-go, negotiation only.
3. **Hard-capped and pre-committed to stop.** $6K / 12 months / 3 gates. It cannot metastasize into a
   focus-draining second job.
4. **No coaching, ever.** The $3.5K–$18K inventRight upsell is the trap that turns a cheap bet into a
   sunk-cost spiral. Free book + free YouTube only.

**Bottom line**: run this as a bounded, mostly-delegated background lottery ticket that respects
CutLog's priority — or don't run it at all. It is a *nice-to-have windfall bet*, explicitly **not** the
secondary income stream Hooman is looking for.
